meta.title: Who really said "Everything is OK in the end. If it's not OK, it's not the end"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lennon. Quote Investigator's earliest match is a 1988 Brazilian book crediting Domingos Sabino; the exact English wording surfaced anonymously in 2000.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everything is OK in the end. If it's not OK, it's not the end'?
meta.ogDescription: Every attribution to John Lennon is posthumous. The oldest known version is Portuguese, written down by Fernando Sabino in 1988 and credited to his father.

answer.label: Not John Lennon — a Brazilian saying, first recorded by Fernando Sabino
answer.sourceLine: The oldest known appearance of this saying is not in English and not by Lennon: Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to the 1988 Brazilian Portuguese book O tabuleiro de damas, where Fernando Sabino credits the line to his father, Domingos Sabino. The exact English wording on this page has no known author at all — Wikiquote ↗ files it under Lennon’s Disputed section and records it circulating anonymously on Usenet in 2000, with the first known credit to Lennon appearing only in 2011.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — Quote Investigator finds every attribution to Lennon is posthumous, and calls those linkages probably spurious.

source.heading: The oldest known version isn't in English

docMeta.dd: Fernando Sabino, crediting his father, Domingos Sabino
From Brazilian Portuguese; English rendering by Quote Investigator (2023)

source.excerpt:
“tudo no fim dá certo. Se não deu, é porque ainda não chegou ao fim.”

Rendered in English by Quote Investigator as: “everything works out in the end. If it didn’t, it’s because it hasn’t come to an end yet.”
trail: 1988 — the earliest citation. Quote Investigator’s earliest match ↗ is Fernando Sabino’s Brazilian Portuguese book O tabuleiro de damas, in which he attributes the saying to his father, Domingos Sabino. The Portuguese wording also appears under Sabino’s name on Portuguese Wikiquote ↗.

2000 — the English sentence, unsigned. Wikiquote ↗ records this exact wording appearing anonymously on the Usenet group alt.support.divorce in 2000, with no author attached. Quote Investigator lists the same 2000 Usenet appearance in its citation timeline.

2011 — the film, then the famous name. Quote Investigator transcribes the variant spoken by Dev Patel’s character in The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel ↗ and notes the saying was already circulating before the film’s release ↗. Wikiquote ↗ dates the first known attribution to Lennon to the same year.

The verdict. Quote Investigator concludes that Domingos Sabino is the leading candidate for creator of the saying on the strength of his son’s 1988 testimony, while allowing that he may have been transmitting an existing adage — and states it has found no citations before 1988 ↗.
source.excerptNote: The English here is Quote Investigator’s rendering of Sabino’s Portuguese, not a published literary translation — and it is not the wording that circulates under Lennon’s name. The familiar English sentence has no identified author.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: Everything Will Be OK in the End

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the familiar English sentence, because it has no identified author or first publication — it is documented circulating anonymously on Usenet in 2000. Separately, the earliest known citation, Fernando Sabino’s O tabuleiro de damas (1988), is a modern work and would be under copyright; the short Portuguese phrase is reproduced here as a brief quotation for attribution research.

author.name: Fernando Sabino
author.heading: The man who wrote it down
author.bio: Fernando Sabino was a Brazilian writer and journalist who published his first book in 1941 and went on to author roughly fifty across his career, winning national and international recognition with O encontro marcado (A Time to Meet, 1956). His claim on this quote is not that he coined it — in the 1988 book O tabuleiro de damas he presents it as something his father, Domingos Sabino, used to say. That secondhand credit is, so far, the oldest documented trace anyone has found of the saying in any language.

misattribution.heading: Four famous names, no evidence
misattribution.intro: This saying has been pinned on a rotating cast of the beloved and the dead. Quote Investigator ↗ examined each and found the same pattern: the attribution always arrives long after the saying is already in circulation.

items.why: Quote Investigator states that the earliest attributions to Oscar Wilde and John Lennon occurred posthumously, and that those linkages were probably spurious ↗. Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Disputed section and records the first known credit to Lennon in 2011. Lennon died on 8 December 1980 ↗.
Named alongside Lennon in Quote Investigator’s ↗ list of attributions that first appear after the attributed speaker’s death, and judged probably spurious on the same grounds.
Quote Investigator notes that attributions to Coelho appear many years after the 1988 citation ↗, which rules him out chronologically as the originator.

items.who: Sonny in The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel (2011)
items.why: Quote Investigator transcribes the film’s version, spoken by Dev Patel’s character, as “Everything will be all right in the end. So if it is not all right, it is not yet the end” ↗ — and observes the saying was already circulating before the film’s release. The film was written by Ol Parker and directed by John Madden ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody can show John Lennon ever said this. The oldest documented version of the thought is Portuguese, written down by Fernando Sabino in 1988 and credited to his father — and even Quote Investigator ↗ allows that Domingos Sabino may simply have been passing along an adage he had heard elsewhere.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Lennon
lead: It is a perfect Lennon-shaped sentence — short, warm, faintly stoned, the sort of thing you can imagine him saying between takes. That is precisely the problem. Feel-good aphorisms drift toward whichever famous name makes them sound wisest, and Lennon, who died in 1980 and can no longer object, is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets.

The saying got its real engine in 2011, when The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel put a version of it in Dev Patel’s mouth as the hotel’s cheerfully doomed manager. But Quote Investigator ↗ notes the phrase was already circulating before the film’s release — the movie amplified it, it did not invent it.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s timeline for this saying runs from a 1920 Buffalo Enquirer item it labels only a thematic match — “There is a happy ending to every story if we only look deep enough for it” — through a dense cluster of 2000s appearances, before the famous-name attributions arrive.

The names that get attached are worth noticing as a set: John Lennon, Oscar Wilde, Paulo Coelho, Fernando Sabino. Three of the four are simply the kind of person the saying sounds like. Only Sabino has a document behind him, and even his document points somewhere else — to his father.
context.pull: The oldest known version is in Portuguese, and the man who wrote it down said he got it from his dad.
